Federal Register — open comment periods
CONSULTATION
US notices with a comment window, searchable and subscribable by email. Thirty to sixty days, and a comment filed inside it must be addressed in the decision. Subscribe rather than check: thirty days is short if you hear on day twenty-eight.
Visit source ↗
EFSA public consultations
CONSULTATION
Every European assessment is published in full with the panel's reasoning and opened for comment, typically for thirty days. The document states what was assessed, which makes it possible to comment on what was not.
Visit source ↗
OGTR — applications open for comment
CONSULTATION
Australia publishes each application, the risk assessment plan and the proposed field sites, then invites comment for around thirty days. Knowing the sites before the decision is what makes a local objection possible.
Visit source ↗
Biosafety Clearing-House — what your country has filed
CONSULTATION
Every party must file its decisions here, and for most first imports intended for release a consultation is required beforehand. For a country with no notice venue of its own this is the only place an application becomes visible in advance — and it is also where to check what a neighbour has decided about the same organism. What a country profile actually holds: the national focal point and competent authorities the country has notified, its national biosafety law where filed, and the decisions it has submitted under Article 20. It is a country's OWN FILINGS, so a thin profile means the country has filed little — not that it decides little. Filing is a treaty obligation without a sanction for missing it.
Visit source ↗
Cartagena Protocol — the right to be consulted
CONSULTATION
Article 23 obliges every party to consult the public in decisions about living modified organisms and to make the results available, while protecting confidential information. Where a country runs no consultation at all, this is the obligation it is not meeting, and citing it by article is more use than an objection with no footing.
Visit source ↗
UN Environment Programme — national biosafety frameworks
CONSULTATION
UNEP helped most countries write their biosafety framework, and the resulting documents — which set out who decides and how the public is involved — are published. For a country whose own ministry publishes nothing, this is often where the procedure is actually written down. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.
